           APPLICATION OF COURT HOUSE POINT ROAD MD PV LLC
         FOR A CERTIFICATE OF PUBLIC CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY

         Court House Point Road MD PV LLC (the "Applicant"), by its undersigned counsel,

hereby submits this Application to the Maryland Public Service Commission (the "Commission")

for a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity ("CPCN") (the "Application") to construct

a 2.5 megawatt alternating current ("MWac") single-axis tracking solar photovoltaic ("PV")

community solar energy generating facility located in Cecil County, Maryland (the "Augustine

Herman Highway Solar Project" or "Project") pursuant to Md. Pqblic Utilities Article ("PUA") §§

7-207 and 7-218

        The Application is comprised of this petition together with the attached Environmental

Review Document ("ERD") and associated appendices. Section 1 of this petition provides an

overview of the Project; Section 2 summarizes how the Project meets the statutory criteria for

granting a CPCN as required by PUA §§ 7-207 and 7-218; and Section 3 summarizes the

Application information required by COMAR 20.79.01.06.




                                      I. PROJECT INTRODUCTION




15251600.1 59715/160448 7/24/26
             The Project is anticipated to occupy approximately twenty (20) acres of an approximately

  28.7-acre property located at Court House Point Road, Chesapeake City, Maryland 21915,
                                                                                                     and
  identified as Tax Map 0048, Grid 0002, Parcel 0003, Parcel ID 02-006073 (the "Propert
                                                                                               y"). The
 Property is located within the Southern Agricultural Residential (" SAR") Zoning District
                                                                                                of Cecil
 County. See ERD § 5.A.

            The Project will be a 2.5 MWac photovo ltaic generating station within the service territory

 of Delmarva Power and Light Company ("DPL"). The Project will interconnect to the
                                                                                                electric
 distribution grid through an existing 34.5 kV feeder back to the utility substation. See ERD
                                                                                                  § 1.
           During the construction phase, the Project is anticipated to provide local economic benefits

 through design, entitlement, construction, and start-up activities. The Project will use
                                                                                                   local
 resources and contractors where feasible, and the Applicant anticipates that the lead contract
                                                                                                  or and
 its subcontractors will comply with prevailing wage standards and provide apprenti
                                                                                                 ceship
 opportunities. Because of the nature of solar installations, environmental and land use
                                                                                               impacts
from the Project will be minimal and the long-tenn benefits significant. See ERD § 5; §7.

           Maryland has established aggressive renewable portfolio standard requirements, requiring

50% of its electricity to be generated from renewable energy sources by 2030, includin g
                                                                                               at least
14.5% solar energy by 2028. In order to meet these goals, Maryland needs commun
                                                                                              ity solar
facilities like the Augustine Herman Highway Solar Project.

           In summary, there are compelling economic, environmental, and legal reasons for the State

and the Commission to expeditiously approve this CPCN application, with no countervail4tg
                                                                                                 harm.
Accordingly, the Applicant respectfully requests that the Commission expeditiously approve
                                                                                                    the
Project.

         When the Commission considers whether to grant a CPCN, it must take into account "the

effect of the generating station ... on :

        (i)    the stability and reliability of the electric system;
        (ii)   economics;
        (iii)  esthetics;
        (iv)   historic sites;
        (v)    aviation safety as determined by the Maryland Aviation Administration and the
        administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration;
        (vi)   when applicable, air and water pollution; and
        (vii) the availability of means for the required timely disposal of wastes produced by any
        generating station."

PUA § 7-207(e)(2). In addition, the Commission must consider "the effect of climate change on

the generating station ... based on the best available scientific information recognized by the

Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change." PUA § 7-207(e)(3). The Commission must

consider:

        (4) for a generating station:
                (i)     the consistency of the application with the comprehensive plan and zoning
                of each county or municipal corporation where any portion of the generating station
                is proposed to be located;
                (ii)    the efforts to resolve any issues presented by a county or municipal
                corporation where any portion of the generating station is proposed to be located;
                (iii)   the impact of the generating station on the quantity of annual and long-term
                statewide greenhouse gas emissions, measured in the manner specified in§ 2-1202
                of the Environment Article and based on the best available scientific information
                recognized by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change; and
                (iv)    the consistency of the application with the State's climate commitments for
                reducing statewide greenhouse gas emissions, including those specified in Title 2,
                Subtitle ·12 of the Environment Article.

        PUA§ 7-207(e)(4).

        Finally, as of July 1, 2025 , the Commission must consider, "for a solar energy generating

station specified under § 7-218 of this subtitle, whether the owner of a proposed solar energy

                                                                                                                  ("SAR" )
    Zoning District. Community based solar is permitted as a special exception with
                                                                                                     conditions in SAR

                                                                                                           requirements,
    including the County 's 300-foot roadway setback, 50-acre minimum parcel
                                                                                                         size, 25% site
    utilization limitation, and soil testing requirements. As of July 1, 2025, Public
                                                                                                     Utilities Article §
    7-218(h)(l)(i) provides that a local jurisdiction may not "adopt zoning laws
                                                                                                      or other laws or
    regulations that prohibit the construction or operation of solar energy generation
                                                                                                     stations ." Further, ·
    Public Utilities Article § 7-218(h)(2)(ii) provides that for solar projects not larger
                                                                                                        than 5 MWac a
    local jurisdiction shall "process [the project's] site development plan as a permitt
                                                                                                      ed use subject to
 the review standards in § 4-205 of the Land Use Article." Accordingly, the County
                                                                                                           is required to
process the Project as a permitted use in this location. See ERD § 5.C.

            The Project is proposing agrivoltaics, and as stated in PUA § 7-218(f
                                                                                                            )(l), certain
requirements prescribed in § 7-218(f) do not apply to agrivoltaics. The Project
                                                                                                          will maintain
approximately 195 feet between the panels and the nearest residential dwellin
                                                                                                    g and at least 100
feet between the solar array and all property lines. See ERD § 5.

           As described throughout the Environmental Review Document, the Project
                                                                                                           is consistent
with Cecil County 's Comprehensive Plan, dated 2010, because it supports County
                                                                                                           policy goals

        The glare analysis prepared for the Project concluded that the Project is not expected to

create significant glare impacts to nearby residences, roadways, or aviation receptors. See ERD §

5.D. The Project will include perimeter fencing and vegetative buffering designed to screen Project

components from surrounding properties and public views, consistent with the siting and visual

mitigation measures described in the ERD. See ERD § 5.E.

        The Project is not expected to adversely affect public safety or transportation because

construction traffic will be temporary, operational traffic will be minimal, and the Project will be

designed and operated in accordance with applicable safety requirements. See ERD § 5.G.

        During operation, noise emissions from the Project are expected to be minimal and

consistent with applicable standards, as evaluated in the Project's noise analysis. See ERD § 7.9;

see also Appendix L.

        Various regulatory agencies, including the Maryland Department of the Environment

("MDE"), Department of Natural Resources ("DNR"), U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service ("USFWS"),

and Maryland Historical Trust ("MHT"), have provided or are expected to provide comments on

the Project' s ability to avoid and minimize environmental impacts. The Project is outside of the

Critical Area, is not located within a Tier II catchment area, and is more than 7.8 miles from the

closest Tier II stream. See ERD § 7.A.4. The Project avoids identified wetlands, and delineated

wetlands will be buffered a minimum of twenty-five (25) feet. See ERD § 6; see also Appendix G.

    Court House Point Road MD PV LLC (the "Applicant") proposes to develop a 2.5 megawatt
    alternating current ("MWac") photovoltaic ("PV") solar system in Chesapeake City, Ceci l Cou nty
    (the "County"), Maryland ("MD"). The Applicant is applying to the Maryland Public Service

    for the Augustine Herman Highway Solar Project ("the Project"). A Conceptual Site Plan for the
    Project is included as Appendix A.

                                                                                         Preface
                                                                                         Soil surveys contain information that affects land use planning in survey areas.
                                                                                         They highlight soil limitations that affect various land uses and provide information
                                                                                         about the properties of the soils in the survey areas. So il surveys are designed for
                                                                                         many different users, including farmers, ranchers , foresters, agronomists , urban
                                                                                         planners, community officials, engineers, developers, builders, and home buyers .
                                                                                         Also , conservationists , teachers, students, and specialists ill recreation , waste
                                                                                         disposal , and pollution control can use the surveys to help them understand,
                                                                                         protect, or enhance the environment.
                                                                                         Various land use regulations of Federal , State, and local governments may impose
                                                                                         special restrictions on land use or land treatment. Soil surveys identify soil
                                                                                         properties that are used in making various land use or land treatment decisions.
                                                                                         The information is intended to help the land users identify and reduce the effects of
                                                                                         soil limitations on various land uses. The landowner or user is responsible for
                                                                                         identifying and complying with existing laws and regulations .

                                                                                         Although soil survey information can be used for general farm, local, and wide r area
                                                                                         planning, onsite investigation is needed to supplement thi s informati on in some
                                                                                         cases. Examples include soil quality assessments (http://www. nrcs .usda.gov/wps/
                                                                                         portal/nrcs/ main/soils/health/} and certain conservation and engineering
                                                                                         applications. For more detailed information, contact your local USDA Service Center
                                                                                         (https://offices.sc.egov.usda.gov/locator/app?agency=nrcs) or your NRCS Slate Soil
                                                                                         Scientist (http://www.nrcs.usda.gov/wps/portal/nrcs/detail/soils/contactus/?
                                                                                         cid=nrcs142p2_053951 ).
                                                                                         Great differences in soil properties can occur within short distances. Some soils are
                                                                                         seasonally wet or subject to flooding . Some are too unstable to be used as a
                                                                                         foundation for buildings or roads . Clayey or wet soils are poorly suited to use as
                                                                                         septic tank absorption fields. A high water table makes a soil poorly suited to
                                                                                         basements or underground installations.
